title: Root Cellar
body:
Root Cellar is a traditional underground or earth-bermed food store that uses the steady cool temperature of the earth to keep vegetables, fruit, and preserves for months. It is built with masonry or timber walls, a ventilated door, and shelving arranged so air moves around stored goods without chilling them to freezing.

Root cellars belong to farm and homestead architecture: they predate electric refrigeration, they are still built today for harvest storage, and their design lesson is passive climate control through earth contact, drainage, and shade.

title: Storm Shelter
body:
Storm Shelter is a small reinforced room or underground chamber built into or beside a home so occupants have a protected place during severe wind and hail. It is anchored to a foundation, fitted with a latched door that opens inward or is protected from debris, and stocked for short stays during a storm warning.

Storm shelters are civilian safety architecture. Their design is governed by published residential shelter guidance, and their purpose is protection from weather, not from any weapon or military system.

title: Tornado Shelter
body:
Tornado Shelter is a purpose-built refuge designed to resist the wind and flying debris of a tornado, usually sited below ground or as an interior safe room with reinforced walls and ceiling. It is sized for a household, ventilated for a short stay, and entered quickly from the living areas of the home.

Tornado shelters are a distinct civilian type within storm architecture, and their history runs from farm storm cellars to modern engineered safe rooms that follow published residential standards.

title: Historical Civil-Defense Fallout Shelter
body:
Historical Civil-Defense Fallout Shelter is a mid-twentieth-century civilian shelter type built in basements, schools, and public buildings during the Cold War, stocked with water, food, and supplies for a stay of days. Its architecture is a matter of public historical record: thick concrete walls, a protected entrance, and a ventilation arrangement for a crowded room.

This record is historical and architectural only. It describes what was built and why communities built it; it gives no instructions for defeating any weapon or defense system, and no such content appears anywhere in this database.

title: Wine Cellar
body:
Wine Cellar is a cool, humid, dark store for wine, built below ground or in a climate-controlled room, with racks that hold bottles on their sides and a stable temperature that changes only slowly through the seasons. Its architecture is about preservation: insulation, humidity control, and still air around the bottles.

Wine cellars range from farmhouse rooms to commercial vaults, and they show how a bunker form — an earth-sheltered, insulated chamber — serves an ordinary civilian pleasure rather than any military purpose.

title: Data Bunker
body:
Data Bunker is a hardened civilian facility that houses computer servers and network equipment, built with redundant power, cooling, fire suppression, and physical access control. It is usually sited underground or in a converted industrial building, and its purpose is keeping information systems running through power cuts, fires, and floods.

Data bunkers are commercial architecture of the internet age. Their design language is redundancy: two of everything that matters, so no single failure takes the facility down.

title: Food-Storage Bunker
body:
Food-Storage Bunker is a large earth-sheltered store for bulk food, grain, and preserves, built for farms, cooperatives, and community food programs. It uses thick insulated walls, controlled ventilation, and dry shelving to hold harvests through winter and to protect stores from pests, damp, and heat.

Food-storage bunkers continue the root-cellar tradition at community scale, and they are a practical part of local food security in regions with long winters or unreliable transport.

title: Earth-Sheltered Dwelling Bunker
body:
Earth-Sheltered Dwelling Bunker is a home built partly or wholly into a hillside or beneath an earth-covered roof, using the ground as insulation and wind protection. Its rooms are daylit from the open side, its roof is planted or gravelled, and its energy use is far lower than a comparable above-ground house.

Earth-sheltered homes are civilian green architecture. They show the bunker form at its most domestic: a quiet, well-insulated house that happens to be built into the land.
